sources: Guarisco 2001, The Journal of Arachnology 29: 267-269, Description of the egg sac of Mimetus notius (Araneae, Mimetidae): mimetids have earned the names assassin and pirate spiders; armed with a series of long, slightly curved spines on legs I and II, they enter spider webs, especially of comb-footed spiders (Theridiidae) and orb weavers (Araneidae), and prey on the occupants; Jackson & Whitehouse (1986) observed mimetids using vibratory aggressive mimicry to lure spiders within striking range; four Mimetus species found in Kansas, M. notius taken on eaves and outer walls of a building; the egg sac hangs inside a thin net of silk; https://www.americanarachnology.org/journal-joa/joa-all-articles/article/download/arac_29_02_0267.pdf

Zhang, Zhang, Liu, Yu & Xu 2025, Zoosystematics and Evolution 101(2): 711-734, A survey of mimetid spiders from Central Guizhou Province, China: instead of building their own webs, mimetids invade other spiders' webs and imitate prey vibrations or courtship signals, a well documented example of aggressive mimicry; prominent rows of raptorial spines on the front legs form a basket that holds the prey; once seen as eating only spiders, they also eat other arthropods; 163 species worldwide; https://doi.org/10.3897/zse.101.146895

beats.say: A spider is creeping onto the web outside your window, to eat the spider that lives there.
The pirate spider. It hunts other spiders.
It plucks the web, like a bug stuck in it, or a male coming to court.
The owner comes to check. And the pirate grabs her, in a basket of spiny legs.
Then it bites, and eats her. Right in her own web.
Its favorite targets? Orb weavers, and cobweb spiders.
It never builds a web to hunt. Why bother, when someone else already did?
